demos.heading: Before you run anything: set up the shell
demos.purpose: DocuMind can answer a tenant's questions from four stores: its own Vector Search index (the ANN tier), the Firestore rung beneath it, or two managed mirrors, Vertex AI RAG Engine and Vertex AI Search. make up pins acme to RAG Engine and zeta to Vertex AI Search so every store the course teaches is exercised. A managed store holds the text of every current version, but not the kit's addresses: its citations come back with ids like acme:acme_497809ff...#rag-532341da71fe, a page of null even for a PDF, and stages.retrieval_backend: rag_engine. This lesson is about the kit's own rows, so point acme at them for the duration and put the pin back at the end. Module 2 compares the four stores; Module 7 studies the mirrors.

demos.heading: One iteration by hand
demos.purpose: Do it: the workspace The second cell plays iteration 1 the way a hurried agent might. It writes the kit's function with one line hard-coded, as seeds.json's placeholder has it. Then it runs the fast test that the prompt names, and asks both oracles about the workspace. Now write the body that spec.md describes, in $WS/shared/desk_calc.py, by hand or with a coding agent under your eye. Gemini CLI started in the workspace with no flags runs in its default approval mode: it asks before every edit and every command. Approve each edit to the function, and decline anything that reaches for gcloud, git or the network. It loads the workspace's GEMINI.md, the loop's notes, which carry that name only inside a workspace: a Gemini CLI session opened in the kit itself never loads them. How Gemini CLI signs in on your machine is your own setup, and nothing else on this page uses it. Then run the fast test and check again.

# Fix plan

One item an iteration: take the first unticked item, do it, then tick it ([x]). When oracle.md lists a failed check
that no item covers, add an unticked item for it at the end.

- [ ] Write statutory_deadline's body, as spec.md says
# The oracle's verdict: FAIL

The strong oracle, on the task as it starts, before any iteration. 10 of its 11 checks failed:

- desk_calc's own selftest: it stopped with NotImplementedError
- the four events s.17(2) counts from are taken, in any case and with spaces around them: statutory_deadline raised NotImplementedError on a question it must answer
- every day of 2026, for each event: the second working day after the last working day, Monday to Friday: 1,460 of 1,460 wrong
- a last working day given as a date is read as its ISO text: statutory_deadline raised NotImplementedError on a question it must answer
- an event s.17(2) does not count from is refused with CalcError: an event outside the four raised NotImplementedError, not CalcError
- a last working day not written YYYY-MM-DD is refused with CalcError: a last working day not written YYYY-MM-DD raised NotImplementedError, not CalcError
- the result: calculator statutory_deadline, the due date as YYYY-MM-DD text, unit date, not an estimate: statutory_deadline raised NotImplementedError on a question it must answer
- the result cites the Code on Wages, 2019, s.17(2) and s.17(3): statutory_deadline raised NotImplementedError on a question it must answer
- the formula shows the last working day, the event and the date due: statutory_deadline raised NotImplementedError on a question it must answer
- the notes say no holiday calendar is loaded, and that s.17(3) may set another time limit: statutory_deadline raised NotImplementedError on a question it must answer
def statutory_deadline(event: str, last_working_day) -> dict:
    """Code on Wages, 2019, s.17(2): wages are paid within two working days of a removal, dismissal, retrenchment or
    resignation. Counted from the person's last working day, as the case queue's exit clock counts it
    (cases.exit_flags), on working days Monday to Friday until a holiday calendar exists (cases.working_days_after)."""
    raise NotImplementedError("statutory_deadline has no body yet: spec.md says what it does")

demos.heading: The reviewer: a linter first, then Gemini on your lane
demos.purpose: Offline, a linter takes the reviewer's seat: a few regular expressions over the diff's added lines, and a check that added code which writes notes names NO_HOLIDAYS. It shows how the score is kept, at Rs 0. The first cell scores it on the seven diffs, and the second runs it on the diff of your hand iteration from step 3. With PROJECT, make review-eval reviews the seven diffs with gemini-3.6-flash on location global, thinking low. It runs as you: a review reads a diff and calls no tool, so it uses your own sign-in, unlike the loop's agent. REPEAT=3 reviews each diff three times, because a model's review differs from run to run. That is 21 calls, about Rs 5.48 of input (each request is 2,042 to 2,054 tokens by the kit's four-characters-a-token count), plus output and thinking, which the kit does not cap. REPEAT=1 costs a third. SAVE keeps every finding with the model and the date, and make review-eval FROM= with that file rescores it at Rs 0.

steps.heading: The reviewer: a linter first, then Gemini on your lane

demos.heading: The live loop: Gemini CLI in a container, on a model-only key
demos.purpose: DRY_RUN=1 prints the two docker run lines an iteration would run, and starts nothing: no Docker, image or key is needed. By default the agent's container can reach whatever the machine it runs on can reach. RALPH_EGRESS=proxy holds it to the model endpoint. Each iteration gets an internal network of its own, which has no route out, and a third container from the same image: commands/ralph/egress.py, an allowlisting forward proxy, on that network and on Docker's default bridge. The agent's container joins the internal network alone, with HTTPS_PROXY naming the proxy. The proxy opens a tunnel to aiplatform.googleapis.com:443 and refuses every other host, port and plain request without dialling it. A tool that ignores the proxy has no route at all, because the internal network has none. The network and the proxy are made before each iteration and removed after it, and the proxy's log, a line a request, is kept in the run's iterations/. The agent's line is the one above with two flags added, --network and HTTPS_PROXY. By default the agent's container can reach whatever the machine it runs on can reach. The proxy opens a tunnel to aiplatform.googleapis.com:443 and refuses every other host, port and plain request without dialling it. A tool that ignores the proxy has no route at all, because the internal network has none. The network and the proxy are made before each iteration and removed after it, and the proxy's log, a line a request, is kept in the run's iterations/. The agent's line is the one above with two flags added, --network and HTTPS_PROXY. The kit's tests run the proxy on your machine's loopback, with a stand-in in place of the model endpoint, and the loop against a stub Docker. A live Docker is the author's check. make ralph-probe RALPH_EGRESS=proxy needs no key and makes no model call. From inside the agent's container it tries example.com and 169.254.169.254, the metadata server's address, directly, then example.com and the model endpoint through the proxy. It also prints whether example.com's name resolved there: whether a name lookup leaves the internal network is Docker's to decide, not the proxy's. Without the author's cap and key, the live loop does not start. It has no default spend, and it runs only on a model-only key, never on your gcloud login or Application Default Credentials.
